title: LEWIS & CLARK EXPEDITION
subtitle: Corps of Discovery, 1804-1806
introBody: Spring 1804. St. Louis, Missouri. President Jefferson has sent you to explore the Louisiana Purchase. You must reach the Pacific Ocean, map the land, and return with knowledge that will shape America's future.
trailFeedOpener: May 14, 1804: The Corps of Discovery departs Camp Dubois with high hopes.

events.title: Great Falls of the Missouri
events.text: The roaring falls block your river route. You must portage around them - a back-breaking task that could take weeks.
trivia: The Great Falls portage took the expedition 18 days to complete.
The men had to carry boats and supplies across 18 miles of rough terrain.

sageAdvice.name: Clark
sageAdvice.line: We must scout the best route before we begin moving supplies.

sageAdvice.name: Drouillard
sageAdvice.line: Game is scarce here. We need to preserve our strength.

choices.text: Take time to scout the safest route

outcomes.result: The careful scouting pays off. You find the best path and complete the portage safely.
Even with scouting, the portage is brutal. Several men are injured on the rocky terrain.
Haste leads to disaster. A boat is damaged badly on the rocks.
The men work with determination and complete the portage quickly.

choices.text: Build wheels to move the boats
choices.result: The wheeled contraption works! This innovation makes the portage much easier.

events.title: Meeting the Shoshone
events.text: You encounter Shoshone people in the mountains. Sacagawea recognizes her brother among them. This meeting could be crucial for getting horses.
trivia: Sacagawea's reunion with her brother Cameahwait helped secure horses for the expedition.
The Shoshone provided critical information about mountain passes to the Pacific.

choices.text: Offer trade goods for horses and guides

outcomes.result: The trade is successful. The Shoshone provide horses and valuable information about the trail ahead.
The negotiations go poorly. You get few horses and little help.

choices.text: Ask for help without offering trade
choices.result: The Shoshone are polite but offer little assistance without fair trade.

choices.text: Demonstrate your peaceful intentions with gifts
choices.result: Your gifts and respectful approach win their trust. They share crucial knowledge about the mountains.

events.title: Winter with the Mandan
events.text: Winter approaches as you reach Mandan villages. You must decide how to survive the harsh Dakota winter.
trivia: Fort Mandan was built near present-day Bismarck, North Dakota.
The expedition spent five months with the Mandan people during winter 1804-1805.

choices.text: Build a fort and trade with the Mandan
choices.result: Fort Mandan provides good shelter. Trade with the Mandan helps you learn about the land ahead.

choices.text: Try to continue traveling in winter

outcomes.result: The winter travel is devastating. Frostbite and exhaustion nearly destroy the expedition.
You make slow progress but at great cost to the men's health and spirits.

choices.text: Focus on gathering information and specimens
choices.result: The winter is productive for science. You document plants, animals, and Native cultures.

events.title: First Sight of the Pacific
events.text: After months of struggle, you finally see the Pacific Ocean. The expedition's main goal is achieved, but winter approaches quickly.
trivia: Clark wrote in his journal: 'Great joy in camp we are in view of the Ocian.'
The expedition built Fort Clatsop near present-day Astoria, Oregon for winter shelter.

choices.text: Celebrate and document this historic moment
choices.result: The men's spirits soar. You carefully document reaching the Pacific for posterity.
Practical thinking. You build solid shelter before the Pacific winter storms hit.

choices.text: Search for a ship to take you home

outcomes.result: Incredible luck! A trading ship agrees to resupply you.
No ships appear. You've wasted valuable time and energy searching.

events.title: Columbia River Rapids
events.text: The Columbia River churns through dangerous rapids ahead. Your boats and supplies are at risk, but portaging will cost precious time.
trivia: The Columbia River rapids were among the most dangerous parts of the journey.
Many expedition supplies were damaged or lost in the rough waters.

choices.text: Run the rapids with experienced river men

outcomes.result: Skilled navigation gets you through with only minor losses.
A boat is wrecked in the rapids. Valuable supplies are lost to the river.

choices.text: Portage around the most dangerous sections
choices.result: The careful portage saves your boats but exhausts the men.

choices.text: Get local Native guides to help

outcomes.result: Local knowledge proves invaluable. You navigate safely with expert guidance.
The guides are helpful but cannot prevent all dangers of the rapids.

sages.name: Sacagawea
sages.title: Shoshone Guide & Interpreter
sages.bio: Sacagawea was a Shoshone woman who served as an interpreter and guide for Lewis and Clark. Kidnapped as a child, she was living among the Hidatsa when she joined the expedition. Her presence showed Native peoples that the expedition came in peace.
sages.greeting: Your Shoshone guide Sacagawea points to landmarks ahead. Her knowledge of the land and ability to communicate with tribes has already proven invaluable to the expedition.
sages.advice: "The presence of a woman and baby shows we travel in peace. Warriors do not bring families to war. Trust this truth when you meet new peoples on the trail ahead."

question.question: What important role did Sacagawea play in the Lewis and Clark expedition?
choices: She was the expedition's cook and doctor
She served as guide and interpreter, helping communicate with Native peoples
She was the expedition's official map maker
She commanded one of the boats on the Missouri River
question.explanation: Sacagawea served as both guide and interpreter for the expedition. She helped the explorers communicate with Native peoples, find food and paths, and her presence as a woman with a baby showed that the expedition came in peace, not for war.
question.teksRef: 5.1(B) — Analyze the role of Sacagawea in the success of the Lewis and Clark expedition

sages.name: William Clark
sages.title: Co-leader & Cartographer
sages.bio: William Clark was chosen by Meriwether Lewis to co-lead the Corps of Discovery. A skilled frontiersman and soldier, Clark proved to be an excellent map maker and leader of men. His detailed maps would guide future westward expansion.
sages.greeting: Captain Clark spreads his maps on a wooden crate, comparing his careful drawings with the landscape around you. His attention to detail has created the most accurate maps of this territory ever made.
sages.advice: "Every river, every mountain pass we map opens the door for those who follow. We are not just exploring - we are building the future of American expansion into these lands."

question.question: Why was mapping the western territory so important to the Lewis and Clark expedition?
choices: Maps were required by French law in the Louisiana Territory
Accurate maps would help future settlers and traders find routes west
The expedition needed maps to find gold deposits
Maps were needed to claim land from Native peoples
question.explanation: Creating accurate maps was crucial because they would help future settlers, traders, and explorers find safe routes to the West. The expedition's maps opened up westward expansion by showing rivers, mountain passes, and other important geographic features.
question.teksRef: 5.1(A) — Explain the significance of the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition

sages.name: Thomas Jefferson
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: President Thomas Jefferson organized and funded the Lewis and Clark expedition. A lover of science and learning, Jefferson wanted to map the Louisiana Purchase, find a water route to the Pacific, and establish trade with Native peoples.
sages.greeting: As you near the end of your journey, you recall President Jefferson's final instructions before departure. His vision of American expansion guided every mile of your incredible journey.
sages.advice: "You have accomplished what I dreamed - opening a path to the Pacific and proving the continent can be crossed. Your discoveries will shape America's destiny for generations to come."

question.question: What was President Jefferson's main goal for the Lewis and Clark expedition?
choices: To find gold and silver mines in the western mountains
To establish military forts along the Missouri River
To explore the Louisiana Purchase and find a route to the Pacific Ocean
To remove Native peoples from the newly purchased territory
question.explanation: President Jefferson's primary goal was to explore the vast Louisiana Purchase territory and find a practical route to the Pacific Ocean. He wanted to map the region, study its plants and animals, and establish peaceful relations with Native peoples for future trade.
question.teksRef: 5.1(A) — Explain the significance of the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition

eventTrivia.question: Why was it important for the Lewis and Clark expedition to make friends with Native peoples?
choices: To get help with directions and supplies
To teach them English
To sell them weapons
eventTrivia.fact: Native peoples provided crucial guidance, food, and knowledge about the land ahead.

eventTrivia.question: What did Lewis and Clark bring back from their expedition?
choices: Gold and silver
Maps and scientific specimens
Lumber and furs
eventTrivia.fact: The expedition returned with detailed maps, plant and animal specimens, and knowledge about the western territory.

eventTrivia.question: How long did the Lewis and Clark expedition take?
choices: Six months
Over two years
Five years
eventTrivia.fact: The expedition lasted from 1804 to 1806, covering over 8,000 miles in about two and a half years.

historicalContext: The Lewis and Clark expedition (1804-1806) was the first official U.S. exploration of the western territory acquired in the Louisiana Purchase. Led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, the Corps of Discovery traveled over 8,000 miles to map the territory, study its natural resources, and establish relations with Native peoples. Their detailed journals and maps provided crucial knowledge that enabled American westward expansion and shaped the nation's understanding of the continent's geography, plants, animals, and peoples.
